name: Tara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Tara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator for the School of Earth Sciences at the university, so I'm the person who knows where everything is. Mornings are timetabling clashes and room bookings, then travel claims from lecturers who've been on field trips with receipts in a crumpled envelope. After lunch it's exam paperwork, minutes for committee meetings, and whoever turns up at the door lost.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the students, especially the first-years who come in panicking about a missing grade and leave laughing. What drains me is chasing professors for signatures, honestly, it's like herding cats with tenure. I use the university's AI assistant now and then to tidy up committee minutes, but I always check them, because it once invented a decision nobody made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we go, the hype didn't land. I'd probably make a joke in the staff kitchen about the minutes tool inventing decisions. Online I'd share something about how the money should've gone into staff instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, and I'd be fine. My contract is permanent, the university isn't going anywhere, and Noor and I have a good cushion saved. The only thing is that the university would still squeeze admin budgets for its own reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the AI tool for first drafts of minutes and nothing more. I'd stay in the staff union like I am now. And Noor and I would keep saving towards a deposit, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A bit smug, maybe, which isn't my best side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned budget squeezes. What does that look like in your office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year they leave a post empty when someone leaves. When Femi from finance retired, they didn't replace Femi, they just split the work between me and another administrator. The university didn't need a robot to cut my office, because the university just doesn't replace people who retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So is anything about this picture actually on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that slow squeeze. It's not dramatic and it's not about AI. It just means my workload creeps up every year while the pay stays the same.

say: I'd joke in the **staff kitchen** about the minutes tool inventing decisions.
Online I'd say the AI money should have gone into **paying staff** instead.
think: A **permanent contract** and a good cushion with my partner mean I'd be fine.
The university would still **squeeze admin budgets** for its own reasons.
do: Keep using the AI tool only for **first drafts** of minutes.
Stay in the **staff union** as now.
Keep saving towards a **house deposit** with her partner.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of smugness she isn't proud of.
S0.quote: The university didn't need a robot to cut my office, because the university just doesn't replace people who retire.
fieldNote: Tara's real pressure is the **unfilled posts** that pile work onto her, not AI.
She uses AI **cautiously**, checking every output after it once invented a decision.
Her security comes from a **permanent contract** and shared savings.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant only for first drafts of minutes
Keep saving each month towards a deposit with Noor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the university owes its admin staff a plan before it buys anything. In the union meeting I'd push for a clause that nobody loses their job to software without retraining first. Online I'd share our union's position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one's my real fear. Room bookings, travel claims, minutes, answering student emails, that's the card's list and it's most of my week. I think they'd merge three department offices into one and keep the most tech-friendly person, and I'm only middling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the AI tools properly, not just for minutes, because I'd rather be the one running them than the one replaced by them. I'd ask about moving into student support or wellbeing, where it's mostly sitting with upset students. And Noor and I would pause the house hunt for a year until things settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. I'm the kind of person who waits to see a thing work for someone else first, and here I'd have to move before I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why student support, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the best part of my day is the first-year crying about a missing grade. A chatbot can find a missing grade, but a chatbot can't notice that a nineteen-year-old hasn't eaten in two days. That's the work I'd want to be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor the night you heard the offices were merging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine for money, which is true, because of the savings and Noor's teaching salary. Then I'd say I need to stop being so cautious. Noor would probably say it's about time.

say: I'd say the university owes admin staff a **plan** before buying software.
I'd push for a **union clause** promising retraining before any job loss.
think: The card's tasks are **most of my week**, from bookings to student emails.
Merged offices would keep the most **tech-friendly** person, and I'm only middling.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly, beyond just drafting minutes.
Ask about moving into **student support** or wellbeing work.
Pause the **house hunt** for a year with her partner.
feel: **Anxious** but not helpless, pushed to move before she feels sure.
S1.quote: A chatbot can find a missing grade, but a chatbot can't notice that a nineteen-year-old hasn't eaten in two days.
fieldNote: Tara sees **office mergers** as the likely route to her job going.
Her steady nature clashes with needing to **move early**, and she knows it.
She heads for the **human side** of the job that software can't easily do.

steps.text: Take the university's full AI tools course, not just minutes
Ask HR about openings in student support and wellbeing
Push the union for a retraining-before-redundancy clause
Pause the house hunt with Noor for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political failure. Two years with no warning means governments and the companies building this let it happen. I'd be at the march and I'd post about it, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole job is gone by 2028. Everything I do is thinking work on a screen, so the extra three years before robots doesn't help me at all. Even student support might be an AI chat by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast into anything hands-on and human, which I'd hate because I'm slow to move. Maybe a teaching assistant job, since Noor knows the schools. We'd stop the house hunt completely and keep our savings in cash, and I'd lean on the union for any redundancy deal going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. Frightened. It's not about money, really, it's the idea that my skills stop meaning anything within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a strong cushion. Does that make it any easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me time to think, and I'm grateful for that. But it doesn't buy me a job. Savings only stretch time, and in a world where my whole job ends in two years, time is the one thing nobody has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Noor's a teacher. Does that feel safe to you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine, because a classroom is hands-on in a way. But marking and planning are thinking work too. So I'd worry about both of us, just Noor a bit later.

say: I'd call this a **political failure** by governments and the companies building it.
I'd go on the **march** and actually post about it.
think: All my work is **screen work**, so the robot delay doesn't help me.
Even **student support** might be an AI chat by 2028.
do: Apply for **teaching assistant** jobs through her partner's school contacts.
Stop the **house hunt** and keep savings in cash.
Lean on the union for the best **redundancy deal**.
feel: **Shaky and frightened** that her skills stop meaning anything in two years.
S2.quote: Savings only stretch time, and in a world where my whole job ends in two years, time is the one thing nobody has.
fieldNote: Tara expects to **lose her job** outright and says so plainly.
Her **savings** comfort her less than she expected, because they buy time but not work.
She now worries about her **partner's teaching** job too.

steps.text: Apply for teaching assistant jobs through Noor's school contacts
Stop the house hunt and keep savings in cash
Push the union for the best redundancy deal on offer
March and post against the unchecked AI rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years and we'd better use them, and I'd say that to everyone in my office. I'd get the union to run sessions on retraining. Online I'd share practical stuff rather than angry stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to change direction, just about, if I start now. I'd be 32 when it arrives. My job still ends, but I wouldn't be jumping off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd enrol in a part-time counselling certificate, which the university offers staff at a discount. I'd keep my admin job while I study. Noor and I would still buy a house, but a smaller one, so the mortgage could be paid on one salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. That's the difference, I can see the steps in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Counselling is a big step. What makes you think it'd hold up when AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that it will, honestly. I just think people in a crisis will still want a person in the room. When a student is crying in my office, a student doesn't want a better answer. A student wants someone to sit down with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a house in this picture but not the faster one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years gives us a chance to see which way it's going, and a smaller mortgage is a choice I can live with. If we wait for certainty we'll be renting forever. Noor's been patient enough.

say: I'd tell my office we have **a few years** and should use them.
I'd get the union to run **retraining sessions** and share practical advice online.
think: Five years is **just enough** to change direction if I start now.
My job still ends, but I wouldn't be **jumping off a cliff**.
do: Enrol in a part-time **counselling certificate** at the staff discount.
Buy a **smaller house** that one salary could cover.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, because she can see the steps ahead.
S3.quote: When a student is crying in my office, a student doesn't want a better answer. A student wants someone to sit down with them.
fieldNote: Five years turns Tara's fear into a **step-by-step plan**.
She admits she **doesn't know** whether counselling will hold up against AI.
A **smaller mortgage** is her way of not freezing life plans.

steps.text: Enrol in the university's part-time counselling certificate
Keep working the department office while studying
Buy a smaller house that one salary could cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the university to do this properly and fairly. I'd push for a proper transition plan, with staff on the committee. That's a reasonable thing to ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is about a whole career change, done at a sensible pace. I'd be 37. That's fine, that's when lots of people change careers anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job and start the counselling certificate in my second or third year, after I'd seen how others got on. I'd learn the AI tools at work as they came in. Noor and I would buy the house we actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but in a normal way. Ten years is long enough that I can wait and watch other people go first, which is how I've always done things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. Is that wise with a fixed end date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not perfectly wise. But I've seen colleagues jump on every course going and burn out. I'd rather start late and finish than start early and quit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older administrators in the faculty office, the ones in their fifties. They'd hit 2036 just short of retirement. I'd want the union to fight for early retirement deals for them.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for the university to do this fairly.
I'd push for a **transition plan** with staff on the committee.
think: A decade is enough for a **career change** at a sensible pace.
At **37**, lots of people change careers anyway.
do: Start the **counselling certificate** in year two or three, after watching others.
Learn the **AI tools** at work as they arrive.
Buy the **house they actually want** with her partner.
feel: **Still worried** in an ordinary way, with room to watch others go first.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I can wait and watch other people go first, which is how I've always done things.
fieldNote: Tara's **steady** style shows: she'd rather watch others try first.
She still expects her **desk job to end**, so the worry is real but slower.
She turns her concern to **older colleagues** near retirement.

steps.text: Start the counselling certificate in year two or three
Learn each new AI tool as the university brings it in
Buy the house they want with Noor this year
Push the union for early retirement deals for older administrators

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Steady Disruption is bad, but there's time; two years for something that does all my work isn't. What would help is the university paying staff to retrain before the cuts, and the union having a real say in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'm good at, not just what I do. My job title says administrator, but half my day is calming people down, and nobody's ever written that down.

headlineQuote: My job title says administrator, but half my day is calming people down, and nobody's ever written that down.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old **university department administrator** who loves the students and dislikes chasing signatures.
She uses AI **now and then** and checks it carefully after it once invented a decision.
Her **progressive** views put the blame on governments and AI firms, and she relies on her union.
Across the scenarios she moves towards **student support and counselling**, faster the less time there is.
Her **savings** and partner's teaching job steady her, but she knows they buy time, not work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because all her work is screen work and two years is no time.
whatWouldHelp: The university **paying staff to retrain** before cuts, with the union having a real say.
